The authors argue that the division of training data into discrete chunks, even in the absence of task shifts, significantly degrades performance compared to learning from the entire dataset at once. This phenomenon, which they term the 'chunking problem,' is demonstrated through empirical evaluations using standard CL benchmarks. The authors show that common CL methods do not effectively address this issue, performing comparably to plain Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when task shifts are absent. Their analysis reveals that the primary cause of this performance drop is not catastrophic forgetting, as is often the case in CL with task shifts, but rather a form of forgetting induced by the chunking process itself. To mitigate this, the authors propose a simple yet effective method: per-chunk weight averaging. This technique involves averaging the model's weights after training on each chunk, rather than relying solely on the final weights after all chunks have been processed. They motivate this approach by analyzing a linear case, showing that weight averaging approximates Bayesian linear regression, which is known to be robust to data fragmentation. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of per-chunk weight averaging across various datasets and show that it improves performance not only in the chunking setting but also generalizes to the full CL setting. This work highlights the importance of considering data chunking as a distinct challenge in CL, separate from task shifts, and offers a practical solution that could be easily integrated into existing CL frameworks.
